story.card_text:
From New Year's Day 1884, the city's sewage came to this granite building to be lifted and sent under the harbor. Before that, Boston's sewers dumped onto the flats around the city. The Board of Health said they produced nine-tenths of all the stenches people complained about, and an 1872 report described a smell 'so strong as to arouse the sleeping.' The fix ran under the ground: intercepting sewers brought the waste out here to Old Harbor Point. Two steam engines designed by Erasmus D. Leavitt lifted it about 35 feet. Each could move 25 million gallons a day and each had a 72.5-ton flywheel. From here a shaft dropped 160 feet to a tunnel cut through bedrock, a mile and a third under the water to Squantum Neck, and on to Moon Island, where the sewage waited in tanks for the outgoing tide.

The architect was George A. Clough, Boston's first City Architect, the same man who restored the Old State House you passed earlier. It pumped until Deer Island took over in 1968. UMass Boston got it in 2011 in exchange for $2.1 million in scholarships. In November 2024 the Landmarks Commission voted to make it a Boston Landmark; Historic Boston reported the vote still needed the mayor and City Council.

story.narration_script: Stand on Mount Vernon Street and look at the rough granite building with the arched door. This is where Boston's sewage went. Before eighteen eighty-four, the city's sewers emptied onto the mud flats, and the Board of Health said they caused nine-tenths of all the stink people complained about. One report described a smell strong enough to wake the sleeping. So the city built this. On New Year's Day, eighteen eighty-four, it started pumping. Two giant steam engines lifted the sewage about thirty-five feet. Each flywheel weighed seventy-two and a half tons. Then it dropped down a shaft a hundred and sixty feet deep, into a tunnel through bedrock under the harbor, more than a mile, out to Moon Island, where it waited for the tide to go out. The architect also restored the Old State House. Look by the door for three letters, B, I, S. Boston Improved Sewer.

story.card_text:
At about 6 a.m. on September 1, 1897, car 1752, in from Allston, rolled down the incline at the Public Garden and into the tunnel. Three minutes later it pulled in under your feet. America had a subway, and this entrance has been collecting plaques about it ever since.

The city's own plaque, in one of the station's exits, reads like a birth certificate: built by the Boston Transit Commission, 'Begun at the Public Garden 28 March 1895,' opened to this point 1 September 1897. In 1964 the National Park Service declared the Tremont Street subway a National Historic Landmark and put up the plaque you just read. The civil engineers added a landmark marker of their own, and in 2004 the IEEE bolted on a third, for the electric power system the West End Street Railway built for Boston's streetcars. In its first full year the subway carried about 50 million rides, by the Landmark nomination's count.

The headhouses are Wheelwright and Haven's, from 1897, reworked twice since. The 1995 round was by Leers Weinzapfel, the same firm that sketched ways to dress the highway chimneys you saw on Atlantic Avenue. Small city.

story.narration_script: You're at Park Street, on the corner of the Common. Find the plaques on the station entrance. At about six in the morning on the first of September, eighteen ninety-seven, a streetcar in from Allston rolled down a ramp in the Public Garden and into a tunnel. Three minutes later it pulled in right under where you're standing. That was America's first subway. Ever since, this entrance has been collecting plaques. The city's own plaque says the work began at the Public Garden on the twenty-eighth of March, eighteen ninety-five. In nineteen sixty-four the National Park Service made the tunnel a National Historic Landmark. The civil engineers added a marker of their own. And in two thousand four the electrical engineers added one more, for the power system that ran Boston's streetcars. In its first full year, the subway carried about fifty million rides. One more thing. These entrances were redone in nineteen ninety-five by the same architects who once sketched ways to dress up the highway chimneys you saw on Atlantic Avenue. Small city.

You walked the mail tube's line backward, from its north end to the old post office, and kept going, past a graveyard that vents a subway, a cellar with a train station in it, a lawn that's a garage roof, a hotel wrapped around two chimneys, a mural wall that only exists to breathe, the corner where the first subway nearly ended before it began, and two streetcars parked on a track that closed in 1962. pitch_60: In eighteen ninety-seven Boston started firing its mail under the streets in steel cans pushed by compressed air. Twenty years later the tubes didn't break down. They lost a vote. Nobody has ever published a photo of a surviving piece. Under Boston is a walk from North Station to the edge of the Common through the parts of the city that run underneath it. America's first subway. A graveyard that breathes for the Green Line. A lawn that's the roof of a seven-floor garage. A hotel built around the highway's chimneys. A mural wall that only exists to breathe. And two old streetcars parked on a dead track inside a station that opened in eighteen ninety-seven. Each riddle walks you to the next spot, and the answer is something you only get by looking. Every story comes with its sources, and a few come with corrections. It starts at North Station. Keep your eyes on the pavement, and bring a CharlieCard for the end.

seo.landing_copy:
Boston built America's first subway in 1897, and most of what it built is still running. Off the Bricks: Under Boston is a self-paced riddle walk from North Station to the Common that follows the city's hidden infrastructure.

You'll solve a riddle, walk to a spot, and find the answer by looking at something real: a street sign, a carved inscription, a pair of chimneys on a roof. Then you get the story, and it's sourced. We read the Boston Transit Commission's annual reports from 1895 to 1905, the federal reports on the pneumatic mail tubes, Big Dig-era Globe reporting and the Greenway's own paperwork. Where the usual story is wrong, we say so and show you who said what.

Along the way: the mail that moved under the streets by compressed air, a graveyard that breathes for the Green Line, a park that is the roof of a seven-level garage, a mural wall that exists to feed air to a highway, a steam plant from 1929, and the corner where the first subway nearly ended before it opened. There's a thirteenth stop for anyone who keeps walking, a short cut of six stops if you've only got an hour, and two detours a T ride away.

About two and a half hours, roughly four kilometers, mostly flat. Start at North Station, end at Boylston. Nothing requires going anywhere you shouldn't: no tunnels, no rooftops, no closed stations. Just the city you walked past, read closely.

story.card_text:
The brick building at 100 Hanover Street looks like a market with offices on top. It is mostly a lung. Built on Big Dig Parcel 7, it holds the ventilation towers for the highway tunnel under your feet, part of Haymarket station, a garage, Registry of Motor Vehicles offices and, since July 2015, the Boston Public Market. Now look down. Asaroton, by Mags Harries, went into this Freedom Trail crosswalk in 1976 for the Bicentennial: bronze market trash, named for the Roman floor mosaics that painted the debris of a banquet. The artists' own notes list crushed cups and the Boston Globe's front page from July 4, 1976. The budget was $10,000. story.card_text:
One of Boston's oldest graveyards has been breathing for the subway since the 1890s. Look through the fence: among the slates is a structure that doesn't belong to anyone buried here. It's a vent for the Tremont Street subway. The subway builders' own photo archive, now at Historic New England, has an 1890s negative titled 'Ventilation structure, King's Chapel Burying Ground, Tremont Street.' The same series has one titled 'Trench machine across King's Chapel Burying Ground.' The headstones themselves were rearranged in the early 1800s and no longer mark the bodies under them.

The Transit Commission's 1899 report lists 'King's Chapel yard' as one of seven ventilating chambers on the line, from the Winthrop School yard to Hanover Street. The fans ran from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and were shut off in damp weather. Professor Henry Carmichael tested the subway air that winter, and the Commission concluded that its busiest station at rush hour had better air than the city's halls, theatres and churches.

Turn toward School Street. The first mail tube ran up it the same year the subway opened, routed on purpose to stay clear of the tunnel. Trains under Tremont, letters under School, both new.

story.narration_script: Look through the fence on Tremont Street, into King's Chapel Burying Ground. Among the old slate headstones there's a structure that doesn't belong to anyone buried here. It's a vent for the subway under the street. The subway builders photographed it in the eighteen nineties, and they photographed something else here too: a trench machine, cutting across the burying ground. In eighteen ninety-nine, the Transit Commission listed this yard as one of seven places where fans pulled air through the tunnel. They ran from seven in the morning to seven at night, and shut off when the weather was damp. A professor tested the air that winter, and the Commission bragged that its busiest station at rush hour beat the air in the city's theatres and churches. Now turn toward School Street. The same year the subway opened, the first mail tube was laid right up that street, routed to stay out of the subway's way. Trains under Tremont. Letters under School.

story.card_text:
In 1903 the floor of the hall upstairs was raised 19 inches to make room for a subway lobby below. The Transit Commission wanted a station under the Old State House, and got one: the eastern half of the basement became a station on the East Boston tunnel, which ran streetcars under the harbor. The Commission's report says the governor inspected the tunnel on December 29, 1904, and the next day it opened 'without further ceremony.' The Massachusetts Historical Society counts 32,000 fares that first day and a seven-minute ride from East Boston to Scollay Square, against 45 minutes to an hour and a half by ferry.

That was as far as the city got. Chapter 385 of the Acts of 1907, 'An Act to Provide for the Preservation of the Old Provincial State House,' barred a second station in the western half and ordered the building restored. The Landmarks Commission's study report says steel beams from the subway work later corroded and helped crack the south wall. The station has been called State since 1967.

story.card_text:
From December 1897, Boston's mail moved by air. Steel cylinders full of letters were shot through underground tubes from the main post office here - a Second Empire building facing the square, half-finished when the 1872 fire swept through and somehow still standing after - up School Street and out to North Union Station. The engineers claimed sixty miles an hour; in daily service it ran nearer thirty, post office to either station in a minute and a half.

The network grew to about seven miles of tube, reaching South Station, Back Bay, Roxbury, Uphams Corner and the Essex Street branch. The tubes didn't fail. They lost a vote. In 1918 the Senate voted to buy them, the House refused, President Wilson vetoed the bill that would have kept them, and the contracts lapsed at the end of June. Boston got its tubes back on August 6, 1926. One history of the system says Senator William M. Butler pressed the button, and the first carrier held an American flag. Congress was still appraising them in 1935 and staffing them in 1939. Boston's own last day of tube mail has never been firmly documented. Neither has a single surviving piece.

story.narration_script: Stand in Post Office Square and look at the pavement. In December of eighteen ninety-seven, the mail started moving under your feet, in steel cans, pushed by air. The main post office faced this square, and the first tube ran from here up School Street to North Station. The engineers bragged about sixty miles an hour. In daily service it was closer to thirty. Still faster than a horse. By the nineteen-tens there were about seven miles of tube under the city. Then, in nineteen eighteen, Washington let it die. The Senate voted to buy the tubes. The House said no. President Wilson vetoed the bill that would have kept them, and the contracts ran out at the end of June. In nineteen twenty-six they came back, and one history says a senator pushed the button that sent an American flag through first. Here's what nobody knows: the last day Boston's tubes ran. And nobody has ever published a photo of a surviving piece.

story.card_text:
There are seven floors of parked cars under this lawn, and they pay for the flowers. Garage revenue covers the park's operations, debt service and property taxes, and in 2014 the Friends of Post Office Square were sending $100,000 a year to a city parks fund and $364,000 to the general fund.

It used to be the other way around. In 1954 the city put a concrete garage in the middle of this square, formally Parking Garage Unit 3. In 1983, nineteen downtown firms formed the Friends and chipped in over a million dollars to get rid of it. They bought the garage and its lease from the city in 1987, started knocking down the 950-space deck on October 1, 1988, and opened the new garage on October 1, 1990: 1,400 spaces, all underground. The park on top was finished in June 1992.

The general manager, Pamela Messenger, told Landscape Architecture Magazine she sells about 2,200 spaces a day and called the place a car day-care center. It's a park that exists because people still drive downtown.

The garage manager once told a magazine she sells about twenty-two hundred spaces a day, and called it a car day-care center. And here's the twist. The cars pay for this park. story.card_text:
At 11:46 a.m. on March 4, 1897, gas that had been leaking into the subway dig here exploded. The Transit Commission's report put it plainly: gas in the space between the subway roof and the temporary bridge carrying the street. A passing streetcar set it off. Six people died at the scene. Four more died afterward. Then the report adds: 'The subway structure was not injured.'

You'll usually read six, including on the City of Boston's archives blog. The Landmark nomination says nine. The Commission's six plus four makes ten, which is BU author Doug Most's count. Some accounts say 11:47.

Then came the lawsuits. The Commission's 1899 report names a test case: Wolf Koplan sued for his injuries, dropped the city before trial, and won a $3,000 verdict against the Boston Gas Light Company, under appeal in 1899.

The subway opened six months later, and the Commission said why it mattered: on the surface, streetcars on Tremont often crawled at two miles an hour. Underground, 282 cars an hour went through at seven or eight. This granite entrance by Wheelwright & Haven is an original; the Landmark nomination notes the pair here and at Park Street were likened to mausoleums. The dig along this edge of the Common also turned up human remains. That story belongs to Bad Ends.

The boxy car behind the fence is No. 5734, built by Brill in 1924 and leased to the T in 1979 for a dollar a year. Sealed under this end of the park is the mouth of a streetcar tunnel about a quarter mile long. On a 2009 tour the Globe found a mound of 1960s fallout-shelter water and biscuit tins inside, and a retired T general manager called it 'about as abandoned as abandoned gets.'

It was the first subway's other front door. One month after the first stretch opened, a four-track portal opened here, in the triangle of Tremont Street, Pleasant Street and Shawmut Avenue, where streetcars dove underground toward Boylston. The usual date is October 1, 1897. The Commission's own 1898 report says September 30, and misprints the year as 1895. The Landmark nomination says this stretch of Pleasant Street is now called Broadway.

Early on, a streetcar historian told the Globe, as many as 100 trolleys an hour came through. He called the steep grade down from Boylston the Boston roller coaster. Service ended April 6, 1962. The portal was sealed, and in 1977 the city dedicated a park on top to Elliot Norton, the long-time Herald theater critic, who hosted Elliot Norton Reviews on WGBH from 1958 to 1982. Nobody gets to walk the tunnel, and you shouldn't try. A park bench on the lid is as close as anyone gets.

subtitle: Mail tubes, ghost platforms and buildings that only breathe
summary: Boston built America's first subway, shot its mail under the streets by compressed air and buried a highway, and most of it is still down there. This one-way walk from North Station to the Common reads the evidence on the surface: a graveyard that vents the Green Line, a lawn that's a garage roof, a hotel built around the highway's chimneys, a mural wall that only exists to breathe. Every stop has a source, and a few have a correction.
title: Under Boston
